title: Uniform bounded-weight Hilbert polynomials and their numerical test
statement:
Fix $r\ge2$, $d>0$, $c\in\mathbf Z$ and $B\ge1$. Let $k$ be any algebraically closed field [def-weil-field] and $X\subset\mathbf P^{r-1}_k$ a closed subscheme [def-weil-closed-immersion] whose homogeneous-coordinate Hilbert polynomial is $P(m)=dm+c$ [def-sfb-projective-coordinate-hilbert-polynomial]. Then $X$ has topological dimension one [def-kun-topological-krull-dimension]. For a basis of linear forms with integral weights $0\le w_i\le B$, define $w_F(m)$ to be the minimum total weight of degree-$m$ monomials whose restrictions form a basis of $H^0(X,\mathcal O_X(m))$ [def-pc-projective-space-twist, def-sc-ringed-space-module-cohomology]. There are $m_0,A\ge1$, depending only on $(r,P,B)$ and independent of $k,X$, the basis and its weights, such that restriction is surjective with target dimension $P(m)$ for $m\ge m_0$, and for each weighted flag $F$ there is $a_F\in\tfrac12\mathbf Z$ with
$$|w_F(m)-a_Fm^2|\le Am\qquad(m\ge m_0).$$
The number $a_F$ depends only on the weighted flag, not its compatible basis. If the $m$th Hilbert point is semistable for [lem-sfb-hilbert-plucker-pgl-linearization], then
$$w_F(m)\le \frac{\sum_iw_i}{r}\,mP(m).$$
No reducedness, purity, connectedness, linear normality or characteristic hypothesis is imposed.

source.place: Section 2.1 Proposition 1 and Lemma 2(1), printed pp.6--8. Agent bounded-weight formulation: the bound depends on B; a bound independent of rescaling all weights would be false. Dimension is the degree-of-Hilbert-polynomial fact in the same Hilbert setup. Local PDF WANTED; read online at https://arxiv.org/pdf/0810.2340.

proof.text: The nonzero polynomial $P(m)=dm+c$, $d>0$, excludes the empty scheme, whose coordinate dimensions are all zero. Apply [lem-sfb-projective-hilbert-polynomial-dimension] to get $\dim X=1$. Apply [lem-sfb-uniform-projective-fibre-vanishing] with $n=r-1$ to choose $M\geq1$ depending only on $r,P$. It gives a coherent $M$-regular ideal sheaf $\mathcal I$, surjective restriction onto $H^0(X,\mathcal O_X(m))$ and dimension $P(m)$ for $m\geq M$. By [lem-pc-projective-space-twist-cohomology], $H^0(\mathbf P^{r-1},\mathcal O(b))=S_b$; $r\geq2$ ensures the cited $n\geq1$ formula applies. The exact restriction sequence identifies its kernel $I_m$ with $H^0(\mathcal I(m))$. Apply the multiplication clause of [lem-sfb-m-regular-coherent-sheaf-consequences] to this coherent $M$-regular sheaf. Iterating its surjections gives $I_m=S_{m-M}I_M$ for $m\geq M$: products of $m-M$ linear coordinate monomials span $S_{m-M}$. Let $J\subset S=k[x_1,\ldots,x_r]$ be generated by a vector-space basis of $I_M$, homogeneous of degree $M$. Then $J_m=I_m$ for $m\geq M$, so $(S/J)_m$ is the required section space in every such degree. Low-degree coordinate equations need not generate $J$ and are not used.

source.place: Section 2.2, Proposition 1 and Lemma 2(1), printed pp.6--8; agent expansion of the bounded-weight estimate by homogeneous initial ideals and finite monomial cells. Local PDF WANTED; read online at https://arxiv.org/pdf/0810.2340.

proof.text: For the given weighted basis order exponents lexicographically by $(|\alpha|,\sum_iw_i\alpha_i,\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_r)$, largest first for leading exponents. The associated increasing order is additive and well-founded: there are only finitely many monomials of any bounded total degree. Apply [lem-sfb-bounded-homogeneous-groebner-degree] to $J$, and put $G=G(r,M)\geq1$. Its initial monomial ideal $K$ is generated by monomials of degree at most $G$, hence with each coordinate at most $G$. These bounds depend only on $r,P$, independently of the basis and the weights. Call a monomial standard when its exponent is outside $K$.

source.place: Dube, The Structure of Polynomial Ideals and Groebner Bases, SIAM J. Comput. 19 (1990), pp.750--773, Theorem 8.2 and Corollary 8.3, printed p.773. Only existence of a degree bound is used; local PDF WANTED, primary article read online. No Stacks tag states this effective bound.

proof.text: The degree-$m$ standard monomials give a basis of $(S/J)_m$. For spanning, divide by the homogeneous family just obtained, using [lem-sfb-monomial-order-polynomial-division], and take the degree-$m$ component of its equality. The remainder consists only of standard monomials. A nonzero linear combination of standard monomials cannot belong to $J$: its leading monomial would both lie outside $K$ and, by the definition of $K$, lie inside $K$. This proves independence. More precisely, division of a degree-$m$ polynomial with all monomial weights at most $s$ gives a remainder of weights at most $s$: the cited order bounds on the products bound their difference from $f$, and our order compares weight within each degree. Consequently, for every $s$, the quotient subspace spanned by monomials of weight at most $s$ has as a basis exactly its standard monomials of weight at most $s$.

source.place: Section 2.2, Proposition 1 and Lemma 2(1), printed pp.6--8; agent expansion of the bounded-weight estimate by homogeneous initial ideals and finite monomial cells. Local PDF WANTED; read online at https://arxiv.org/pdf/0810.2340.

proof.text: It follows that the sum of standard monomial weights equals the minimum weight of a monomial basis. Indeed, if the ordered weights of the standard basis are $a_1\leq\cdots\leq a_N$ and those of any other monomial basis are $b_1\leq\cdots\leq b_N$, then $b_j<a_j$ would give $j$ independent vectors in the weight-$b_j$ subspace, whose dimension is less than $j$ by step 3. Thus $b_j\geq a_j$ for every $j$, and the standard basis attains the minimum. This also proves basis independence: the weight-$s$ subspace of $S_m$ is the span of products from the linear-form subspaces of the given flag with total weight at most $s$, so is unchanged by any change of compatible basis. Its quotient filtration, its dimensions, and therefore the list $(a_j)$ and $w_F(m)$ are unchanged.

source.place: Section 2.2, Proposition 1 and Lemma 2(1), printed pp.6--8; agent expansion of the bounded-weight estimate by homogeneous initial ideals and finite monomial cells. Local PDF WANTED; read online at https://arxiv.org/pdf/0810.2340.

proof.text:
Partition $\mathbf N^r$ into cells by choosing $T\subseteq\{1,\ldots,r\}$, setting $\alpha_i\geq G$ for $i\in T$, and fixing each other coordinate at an integer $\beta_i<G$. A generator of $K$ has all coordinates at most $G$, so whether it divides $x^\alpha$ is constant on each cell. Hence each cell is wholly standard or wholly nonstandard. A standard cell is $\gamma+\mathbf N^T$, where $\gamma_i=G$ on $T$ and $\gamma_i=\beta_i$ otherwise. Write $e=|\gamma|\leq rG$, $z=\sum_iw_i\gamma_i\leq BrG$, and $t=|T|$. If $t\geq3$, its degree-$m$ monomial count grows at least quadratically (choose arbitrary exponents on three free variables summing to $m-e$); it cannot be bounded by the total count $dm+c$ for all large $m$. Thus every standard cell has $t\leq2$. Cells with $t=0$ disappear for $m>rG$. With $n=m-e\geq0$, a cell with $T=\{i\}$ contributes weight $z+w_i n$, and one with $T=\{i,j\}$ contributes
$$z(n+1)+(w_i+w_j)n(n+1)/2.$$
These formulas follow by listing the $n+1$ pairs $(a,n-a)$ and summing $a=0,\ldots,n$.

source.place: Section 2.2, Proposition 1 and Lemma 2(1), printed pp.6--8; agent expansion of the bounded-weight estimate by homogeneous initial ideals and finite monomial cells. Local PDF WANTED; read online at https://arxiv.org/pdf/0810.2340.

proof.text: There are at most $C=(G+1)^r$ cells. For $m\geq\max(M,rG+1)$, summing the formulas in step 5 gives $w_F(m)=a_Fm^2+b_Fm+c_F$. Each two-variable cell contributes $(w_i+w_j)/2$ to $a_F$, and each one-variable cell contributes zero, so $a_F\in\tfrac12\mathbf Z$. Put $H=rG$. Expanding the same formulas gives $|b_F|\leq CB(1+3H)$ and $|c_F|\leq2CB(H+1)^2$: for a two-variable cell the coefficients are $z+(w_i+w_j)(1-2e)/2$ and $z(1-e)+(w_i+w_j)(e^2-e)/2$; the one-variable case has coefficients $w_i$ and $z-w_ie$. Choose the integer $A\geq10BC(H+1)^2$, rounding up if needed. Then $|w_F(m)-a_Fm^2|\leq Am$ for all such $m\geq1$. The constants are uniform because $G$ depends only on $r,P$ and the weights are bounded by $B$. Step 4 and uniqueness of the leading coefficient of an eventual quadratic show that $a_F$ depends only on the flag.

source.place: Section 2.2, Proposition 1 and Lemma 2(1), printed pp.6--8; agent expansion of the bounded-weight estimate by homogeneous initial ideals and finite monomial cells. Local PDF WANTED; read online at https://arxiv.org/pdf/0810.2340.

proof.text:
Increase $m_0$ also to the uniform Hilbert embedding bound of [lem-sfb-hilbert-plucker-pgl-linearization]. Its equality of semistable loci lets us work with $\operatorname{SL}_r$ and $\Lambda_m$. Put $s=\sum_iw_i$ and $v_i=rw_i-s$, so $\sum_iv_i=0$. On degree-$m$ monomials this replaces weight $u$ by $ru-ms$; on a determinant basis it replaces weight $W$ by $rW-msP(m)$. The determinant coordinates are nonzero precisely when their monomial restrictions form a basis, because their values are the corresponding maximal minors of the section quotient. Therefore their minimum centered weight is
$$v_{\min}=r w_F(m)-msP(m).$$
The determinant line and the closed Pluecker embedding are precisely those supplied by the cited node.

source.place: Section 2.2, Proposition 1 and Lemma 2(1), printed pp.6--8; agent expansion of the bounded-weight estimate by homogeneous initial ideals and finite monomial cells. Local PDF WANTED; read online at https://arxiv.org/pdf/0810.2340.

proof.text:
Here is the needed direction of the numerical test directly from the definition of semistability; no stability-only criterion is invoked. Use the inverse of the diagonal one-parameter subgroup with weights $(v_i)$ on linear forms, so its orbit on quotient Pluecker coordinates is $p_Q↦t^{v_Q}p_Q$, where $v_Q$ is the centered monomial-basis weight (the inverse is needed because the group acts on a quotient by precomposition). If $v_{\min}>0$, choose a nonzero coordinate vector $p=(p_Q)$ for the Hilbert point. The normalized vector $(t^{v_Q-v_{\min}}p_Q)_Q$ is regular and nonzero at $t=0$, since $v_Q\geq v_{\min}$ whenever $p_Q
e0$. Its projective morphism lands in the Hilbert scheme: on $t
e0$ it is the group orbit, and all equations of the closed embedding still vanish at $0$. A semistable point has an invariant regular section $\sigma$ of some $\Lambda_m^{\otimes N}$, $N>0$, nonzero there, by [lem-sfb-hilbert-plucker-pgl-linearization]. Pull this section back along that morphism and trivialize by the displayed normalized tautological vector (and its dual for $\mathcal O(1)$). Invariance shows that its coefficient on $t
e0$ is $t^{-Nv_{\min}}\sigma(p)$: evaluation on the inverse-subgroup translate of $p$ equals $\sigma(p)$, and the normalization multiplies degree-$N$ evaluation by $t^{-Nv_{\min}}$. This has a pole at $0$, contradicting regularity and $\sigma(p)
e0$. Hence $v_{\min}\leq0$, which is exactly $w_F(m)\leq (s/r)mP(m)$. All arguments use field linear algebra and integer exponents, so hold in every characteristic.
